stemBlocks.value: The vectors p and q are given: p has components −6 and 9, and q has components 2 and −3. (a) Find the scalar k such that p = kq. (b) State TWO geometric relationships between p and q.
Think first: If one vector is a multiple of another, the same multiplier must work for both components.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p179-q04 from workbook page 179.

solutionSteps.instruction: Interpret the fact that k exists.

contentBlocks.value: One vector is a scalar multiple of the other
Result: p and q are parallel
Result: p and q point in opposite directions
Result: p is three times as long as q

strategyBlocks.value: Divide corresponding components to find k, confirm it works for both, then interpret the sign and size of k geometrically.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) k = −3  (b) Two relationships: p and q are parallel (each is a scalar multiple of the other), and they point in opposite directions with p three times as long as q

whyThisWorks.value: Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches it without changing the line it lies along, so any pair related by p = kq must be parallel. The sign of k records the direction — negative means reversed — while its size records the stretch factor. That is why a single number k captures both geometric facts at once.

commonErrors.misconception: Getting k from one component and not checking it fits the other.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Getting k from one component and not checking it fits the other.

commonErrors.misconception: Saying the vectors point the same way because they are parallel, ignoring the negative sign.

examTip.value: Whenever you find a scalar k linking two vectors, note two things at once: parallel (always), and same or opposite direction (from the sign of k).
